newsitem.title: USA: U.S. government changes leave Middle East adrift.
newsitem.headline: U.S. government changes leave Middle East adrift.

text.p: An impending change of guard at the U.S. State Department is adding to the sense of drift in the Middle East, as ties between Israel, the Palestinians and Syria become increasingly frayed, U.S. analysts say.

Although President Bill Clinton was re-elected on November 5, his foreign policy team looks set for a wholesale shake-up that could have important repercussions for the peace process that Washington has sponsored for the past five years.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher has already announced that he will resign, and no successor has yet been named. Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern Affairs Robert Pelletreau is also expected to leave, and National Security Adviser Tony Lake may move on too.
The plans of special Middle East coordinator Dennis Ross, who has already served both Republican and Democratic administrations, are unclear, colleagues say.

The most obvious symptom in the region of the uncertainty in Washington has been the failure so far of key talks between Israel and the Palestinians to reach agreement on a partial Israeli troop withdrawal from the West Bank town of Hebron.

Ross, who fruitlessly moderated the talks for three weeks, flew home in early November and has refused to go back as the parties bicker over a proposed Israeli right to pursue guerrilla suspects into PLO-controlled parts of the town.

Meanwhile, the six-month-old right-wing government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pushed ahead with plans to expand Jewish settlements in the West Bank and on the occupied Golan Heights, infuriating Arabs.
Some U.S. analysts think these moves are merely to compensate settlers for an eventual pull-back in Hebron, where 400 Jews live among 100,000 Arabs.
In any case, the State Department has done no more than reiterate its standard mild rebuke that settlements are "unhelpful," as officials wait to see what will become of U.S. Middle East policy.

"Clearly, the stagnation in the peace process is not helped by (the hiatus in Washington), and it depends what role the U.S. is going to play and who is going to be in the new foreign policy team," says Judith Kipper of the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.
The uncertainty could continue for nearly two months if Christopher carries out his apparent intention of staying in office until the formal turn of administration January 20.
Much then will depend on who steps into his shoes.
Of the candidates being talked about, Middle East watchers think revolutionary new approaches are unlikely to come from either former Sen. George Mitchell or U.N. ambassador Madeleine Albright.

Some hold out hopes for former Assistant Secretary of State Richard Holbrooke, whose head-banging tactics succeeded in forcing a peace agreement in Bosnia a year ago. But Holbrooke's bruising manner may rule him out of the job.

Whoever it is, Kipper said, "Clearly the new secretary of state is not going to want to repeat the experience of Christopher", whose dozens of trips to Jerusalem and Damascus and cautious, consensus-building approach failed to clinch a deal between Israel and Syria.
The risk will be, Kipper and other analysts believe, that because the Middle East at present does not directly threaten American interests, it could be left to fester.

Although no U.S. administration can afford to ignore the Middle East, a president already focused heavily on domestic issues may find his foreign agenda dominated by such problems as Bosnia, China and world trade.
Already, Washington has signalled it sees no point, for now, in pursuing the Israel-Syria track.

U.S. officials now believe Syrian President Hafez al-Assad was not ready to strike a deal even with Israel's former Labour Prime Minister Shimon Peres, who was prepared to trade land for peace, let alone with Netanyahu, who is not.

Instead, the focus in recent months has been on salvaging the talks between Israel and the Palestinians, which have brought limited Palestinian self-rule in the West Bank and Gaza since the breakthrough Oslo accord of 1993.

Until armed clashes between the two sides broke out in September, the United States had largely stood aside from those talks, arguing that the parties were now on sufficiently good terms to negotiate for themselves.

The new U.S. foreign policy team will have to decide, analysts say, whether to persist with that approach or to adopt a more robust, hands-on policy in a bid to avert a new explosion of violence down the road.
